name: Securitized And MBS
summary: A bond backed by a pool of loans or receivables: ABS, RMBS/CMBS, CLOs, covered bonds and CDOs, usually sliced into tranches that absorb losses from the equity piece upward. Most recommendations turn on one question: can this investor accept liquidity at the bottom of the fixed-income sub-sector ranking, bracketed with EM, and, for the pass-through instruments RMBS, CMBS and amortizing ABS, cash flow timing the borrower controls, in exchange for spread it has the resource to analyse. Covered bonds are the exception to the timing half: they are bullet bank senior debt whose dual recourse and asset substitution keep the collateral's timing with the issuer.

pros.text: Spread from collateral the corporate bond market does not offer. ABS, RMBS/CMBS, CLOs, covered bonds and CDOs are alternatives or complements to corporate bonds, so they can add excess return other than more of the same corporate issuer risk already in the portfolio. Hold the claim to the real-estate and consumer collateral: CLO collateral is leveraged corporate loans, so it diversifies within corporate credit rather than away from it, a CDO of corporate bonds gives no collateral diversification at all, and a covered bond's first recourse is the issuing bank's own credit.

Tranching lets the investor choose the risk point on one collateral pool. Losses are absorbed from the bottom up, the equity tranche first and the senior tranche last, so senior, mezzanine and equity are three different risk assets built from the same loans and the investor can pick a precise point on the risk-return spectrum.

Often a higher yield than similarly rated corporate bonds, in ABS, CMBS, non-agency RMBS and CLOs, which is payment for complexity, model risk, prepayment uncertainty and thinner trading rather than alpha. Covered bonds are the exception: dual recourse means lower credit risk and a lower yield than ABS or MBS.

Covered bonds carry dual recourse, a claim on the issuing bank and on a ring-fenced cover pool whose non-performing assets the bank must substitute out, so they carry lower credit risk, and therefore a lower yield, than ABS or MBS on comparable collateral.

Securitized is one of the standard sectors inside a broad aggregate bond index, which spans Treasuries, agencies, corporates, MBS, ABS and CMBS, so a portfolio benchmarked to such an index while holding no securitized exposure is running an active sector bet, intended or not, rather than a neutral position, and the gap shows up as tracking error. Enhanced indexing matches sector and quality weights, key-rate durations and convexity.

CLO tranches sit on floating-rate leveraged loan collateral, so the coupon rises with the reference rate and the tranche carries little interest-rate duration. It keeps its full spread duration: the spread change times spread duration term in the excess-return and DTS calculation is untouched, so a spread-widening scenario still hurts. Floating coupon is not a low-risk way to take spread.

cons.text: Complexity and model risk. Value depends on prepayment, default and recovery models, and the output is only as good as assumptions and historical relationships that can break.

MBS carry prepayment risk and extension risk, and they bite in both directions. Rates fall, borrowers refinance and principal returns to be reinvested at the lower yield. Rates rise, prepayments slow and the holder is left with a longer bond at a falling price.

Senior tranche safety rests on correlation assumptions about the collateral, and those assumptions failed badly in 2008, so do not treat a highly rated tranche as risk equivalent to a same-rated corporate bond. Know the direction the exam keys: when default correlations rise, the value of the mezzanine tranche rises by more than the senior tranche's, so the trade on an expected correlation rise is short the senior class and long the mezzanine.

Low liquidity. The ranking to quote is sovereign, then investment grade, then high yield, then securitized and EM together at the bottom, so expect wide bid-ask spreads, difficulty trading in size and real transaction costs both ways.

Negative convexity from the prepayment option the borrower holds. Price gains are compressed in a rally while losses in a selloff are not, and effective duration shortens as rates fall and lengthens as rates rise, so a duration or BPV hedge drifts and has to be rebalanced.

Pool diversification is a normal-times property. Separately from the correlation point above, a thin mezzanine tranche is levered to its attachment point, so realized pool losses that still look modest in total can write it down heavily.

whenToRecommend: Total-return credit mandate, corporate spreads described as tight or fully valued, and the manager still needs excess return: structured instruments add spread without simply adding corporate beta or going down in quality. Keep the collateral claim honest: RMBS, CMBS and ABS reach real-estate and consumer cash flows, while CLOs and CDOs add spread from corporate collateral.
The benchmark is a broad aggregate index that includes a securitized sector and the question is tracking error: hold or proxy the sector and match its key-rate durations and convexity.

The investor states a precise risk appetite on a pool of collateral, either the safest claim on it or deliberately the first-loss piece: tranche selection delivers that point on one set of loans without changing asset class.

The manager expects interest-rate volatility to fall, or the vignette is explicitly a volatility view: buy agency MBS. Holding MBS is being short the prepayment option, so a decline in expected volatility lowers that option's value and lifts the bond, with minimal credit risk. Buying MBS is a bet on lower volatility, never higher. Separately, if short rates are rising, prefer a CLO tranche to a CDO tranche, because CLO collateral pays a reference rate plus a spread.

A long-horizon holder with no liability-matching claim on the assets, a savings-type sovereign wealth fund, an endowment or foundation, or the return-seeking sleeve of a long-horizon pension, with the analytical resources to model prepayments and the waterfall: it can demand and earn the liquidity premium because it will not be forced to sell. Not an insurer's reserve portfolio, which is the canonical duration and cash-flow matcher and faces forced sales on disintermediation exactly when MBS extends, and not a plan's liability-hedging sleeve, which grows as funded status improves.

The investor wants exposure to a bank's mortgage or public-sector book with recourse to the bank as well as to the loans: covered bonds, whose dual recourse and substitution of non-performing assets buy lower credit risk, and therefore a lower yield, than ABS or MBS.
whenNotTo: The mandate is cash-flow matching or immunizing a dated liability. Amortizing cash flows whose timing the borrower controls break the match, so use government bonds or a non-callable bullet instead, which is also the minimum-dispersion structure immunization wants.

The portfolio must stay liquid, faces redemptions, caps illiquid holdings, or needs the exposure put on and taken off quickly. Use the liquid proxies instead: government bond futures, bond ETFs, on-the-run bonds and CDS.

The view is a large rate move in either direction, or rising rate volatility. Negative convexity loses against a non-callable bond of the same duration for a large move either way, and the holder is short the prepayment option, so prefer a non-callable government bond. If the volatility view itself is what must be expressed, raise convexity with a barbell or long options and swaptions. Do not reach for a bullet here: a bullet is the low-convexity, sell-convexity structure for a calm market.

The view is specifically about corporate credit spreads or one sector's issuers. Express it in investment-grade corporates, high yield or CDS, which are cleaner and more liquid for that view and carry no structure risk.

The IPS bars complex instruments, or neither manager nor client can model prepayment and the deal waterfall. The answer is investment-grade corporates, where the analysis is issuer credit rather than structure.
pitfalls: Treating a AAA tranche as equivalent to a AAA corporate bond. The notes say this in as many words: do not treat a highly-rated tranche as risk-equivalent to a same-rated corporate bond, because the rating does not capture the correlation and model risk inside the structure.
Calling the yield pickup alpha or free yield. Name what it compensates for, complexity, model risk, prepayment risk and illiquidity, or the point does not score.
Getting the liquidity ranking wrong. It is sovereign, then investment grade, then high yield, then securitized and EM at the bottom. Securitized sits below high yield, not above it.
Naming prepayment risk and stopping. Extension risk is the other half and the marker wants both directions.

Recommending MBS to immunize or cash-flow match a liability. Uncertain, amortizing, borrower-controlled cash flows break the match, and effective duration moves as rates move, so the duration condition will not hold.

Describing a covered bond with ABS risks. It is bank senior debt backed by a ring-fenced mortgage or public-sector pool, the assets stay with the issuing bank, non-performing assets are substituted out, and the recourse is dual, which is why both the credit risk and the yield are lower than ABS or MBS.

cues.signal: Corporate spreads are at or near historic tights, or described as fully valued, but the mandate still requires excess return.
cues.implication: This is the structured-instruments question. Rules in RMBS/CMBS and ABS for spread from collateral the corporate market does not offer, real estate and consumer loans. CLOs and CDOs are not that argument: their collateral is corporate loans or bonds, so they add spread within corporate credit, and a CDO of corporate bonds adds no collateral diversification at all. Say the pickup compensates for complexity, model risk and illiquidity.

cues.signal: The client expects a significant rate rally, or the vignette mentions rising implied rate volatility.
cues.implication: Rules MBS out as the way to express it. Negative convexity compresses the rally gain, effective duration shortens just as you want it long, and the holder is short the prepayment option so higher volatility costs it. A long non-callable government bond captures a rally. If the signal is rising volatility rather than a rally, the convexity answer is a barbell or long options, never a bullet.

cues.signal: A fixed amount due on a stated date, dedication, cash-flow matching, or a Macaulay duration set equal to a horizon.
cues.implication: Rules MBS out as the matching asset, for two different reasons. Cash-flow matching needs certain cash-flow timing, and prepayment puts that timing in the borrower's hands. Immunization fails on its own conditions: with rate-dependent cash flows you are on effective duration rather than a reliable Macaulay duration, effective duration shortens as rates fall and lengthens as they rise so duration equal to the horizon will not hold between rebalances, and negative convexity cannot meet the requirement that asset convexity sit just above the liability's.

cues.signal: The benchmark is a broad aggregate index and the portfolio holds no securitized exposure.
cues.implication: This is a sector-weight and convexity mismatch, so it is tracking error, not a free decision. Securitized is roughly a third of a US aggregate index, so the unintended underweight is large. Enhanced indexing matches sector, quality, key-rate durations and convexity.

cues.signal: The vignette gives a credit view on collateral the portfolio already holds: an expected recovery or lower-than-expected defaults, or a housing-led slowdown.
cues.implication: Rules in a move along the tranche stack rather than out of the asset class. On an expected recovery move down in tranche, because lower-rated tranches tighten more. On a housing-led slowdown move up within MBS, for example a BBB tranche to an A tranche, which keeps the real-estate cash flow exposure while cutting exposure to the greater spread widening of the lower-rated tranche.

cues.signal: The collateral is a bank's own mortgage book and the investor wants recourse to the bank as well as to the loans.
cues.implication: Rules in a covered bond, not RMBS. Dual recourse is the distinguishing feature: the issuing bank plus a ring-fenced cover pool.

cues.signal: The vignette says agency or government guaranteed, rather than non-agency or private label.
cues.implication: Changes which risk you discuss. Agency MBS is a prepayment and convexity story with minimal credit risk. Non-agency MBS, ABS and CLOs add collateral credit risk plus structure and servicer risk, so the analysis must cover the waterfall and the credit enhancement, not just the pool.

deleted: Repair pass. whenNotTo: "The only argument offered is the higher yield and the vignette gives the investor no illiquidity capacity and no analytical resource. The pickup pays for risks this investor cannot carry." Deleted as padding: the liquidity condition and the cannot-model-the-waterfall condition are already two separate items in the same list, so this added no new vignette situation.

Repair pass. pitfalls: "Listing diversification with no reason. The reason is the collateral: consumer loans, mortgages and corporate loans behave differently from corporate credit, and that is what diversifies." Deleted because it restates pros[0] as a writing instruction rather than naming a distinct marking error, and its claim that corporate loan collateral diversifies away from corporate credit is the overstatement pros[0] had to be corrected for.

Skeptic pass. cues[1]: "The IPS requires the ability to meet redemptions, caps illiquid holdings, or the portfolio may need a quick tactical change in exposure" / "Rules securitized out or caps it, because it is the least liquid sub-sector. Rules in the liquid proxies: government bond futures, bond ETFs, on-the-run bonds and CDS." Deleted as a near word-for-word duplicate of whenNotTo[1], same trigger, same four-item proxy list, same conclusion. whenNotTo[1] now carries the "caps illiquid holdings" trigger it was the only thing the cue added. Deleting it also removed a second copy of the "least liquid sub-sector" overstatement, so the liquidity ranking is now stated three times in the entry rather than four, each time doing a different job: cons[3] the fact, pitfalls[2] the marking error, summary the screening gate.

Skeptic pass. pros[1]: dropped the clause "while interest and principal are paid from the top down". The loss ordering is verbatim in the notes, but the direction of the cash flow waterfall is not in the notes, the flashcards or the question bank, and the clause was the only part of pros[1] blocking restoration of the reading citation.

Skeptic pass. The residual risk about agency MBS trading through a same-rated corporate was dropped rather than written into the text. It is market convention, not in the candidate's material, and pros[2] is now scoped to ABS, CMBS, non-agency RMBS and CLOs, which removes the need for it.
corrected: Repair pass. pros[0]: narrowed the diversification claim and added the CLO caveat. The draft said the exposure "is not another bet on the same corporate issuers", which is wrong for CLOs, whose collateral is leveraged corporate loans, so it diversifies within corporate credit rather than away from it.

Repair pass. pros[1] (tranching): cut the claim that holding a corporate bond means taking "one issuer's whole capital structure", which is not true: a corporate bond is itself one point in that capital structure.

Repair pass, RETRACTED by the skeptic pass. The repair pass re-sourced pros[1], pros[2] and pros[3] from fixed_income_active_management_credit_strategies to "curriculum" on the stated ground that the reading "says nothing about a yield pickup over corporates or about dual recourse", and stripped "and the notes say so in as many words" from pitfalls[0] on the same ground. All of that was false. The reading states every one of the four: "Yield pickup, often a higher yield than similarly-rated corporates, compensating for complexity and liquidity"; "Each is TRANCHED so losses hit the equity tranche first and the senior tranche last"; "COVERED BONDS are issued by banks with dual recourse to the issuer AND a ring-fenced cover pool"; and "do not treat a highly-rated tranche as risk-equivalent to a same-rated corporate bond". The repair pass was reading grounding.json's slice for this key, which omits that whole LOS section. Citations restored on pros[1], pros[2] and pros[3], and the notes attribution restored in pitfalls[0]. Both skeptics flagged this independently.

Repair pass. cons[3]: replaced "lowest liquidity of the fixed-income sub-sectors, below high yield" with the ranking the notes actually give, sovereign then investment grade then high yield then securitized and EM.
Repair pass. cons[4]: "price gains are capped in a rally" corrected to compressed. Negative convexity mutes the rally gain, it does not impose a hard cap.

Repair pass. whenToRecommend[2]: dropped "a single corporate bond cannot". A corporate bond does offer a defined risk point; the real distinction is choosing the risk level on one pool of collateral without changing asset class.

Skeptic pass. whenNotTo[2] and cues[2]: the convexity direction was inverted in both. The old text offered "a government bond or a bullet" and "a non-callable government bond or a bullet" as the answer to a trigger that includes rising rate volatility, but in yield_curve_strategies a bullet is the low-convexity, sell-convexity, expect-calm structure: "Expect HIGHER volatility, INCREASE convexity (a barbell, or buy options)" and "Expect LOWER volatility, REDUCE convexity (a bullet, or sell options)", with the worked bullet C=50 versus barbell C=90 example concluding "buy convexity (barbell) when you expect big moves, sell it (bullet) when you expect calm". Both now name a non-callable government bond for the level view and a barbell or long options for the volatility view, and say explicitly not to reach for a bullet. Note that whenNotTo[0] still names a non-callable bullet, correctly: immunization genuinely wants minimum dispersion and convexity. The two uses are now distinguished in the text.

Skeptic pass. cons[2] and cons[5]: the correlation mechanism was pointed at the wrong tranche. cons[5] read "A macro shock hits every borrower at once, and a mezzanine tranche is levered to the pool's losses", welding a correlation story to the mezzanine. The question bank keys the opposite: "when default correlations increase, the value of the mezzanine tranche of a CDO increases by more than the value of the senior tranche", and the keyed trade on an expected correlation rise is short the senior Class A and long the mezzanine Class B. The two mechanisms are now split. cons[2], which already owned the correlation point, gained the keyed direction and the trade. cons[5] keeps only the distinct mezzanine mechanism, leverage to its attachment point on realized losses, with no correlation framing. Both skeptics flagged this independently.

Skeptic pass. whenToRecommend[4]: the archetypes were wrong and contradicted this entry's own whenNotTo[0] and pitfalls[4]. The draft offered "an insurer or a well-funded pension". Per portfolio_management_for_institutional_investors, life insurers "match them with long-duration, high-quality fixed income via duration and cash-flow matching" and face disintermediation, "policyholders surrendering and withdrawing when rates rise, forcing asset sales at a loss", which is exactly when MBS extends and falls, so "it will not be forced to sell" was false for the named holder; P&C insurers "have shorter, lumpier, less predictable claim liabilities, so they hold more liquidity". A well-funded pension is also the wrong direction, since the de-risking glide path moves a plan toward liability-hedging assets as funded status improves. Replaced with the notes' own long and illiquid archetypes, a savings-type SWF, an endowment or foundation, or a long-horizon pension's return-seeking sleeve, and the insurer case is now named as the whenNotTo case instead. Both skeptics flagged this independently.

Skeptic pass. whenToRecommend[3]: replaced. The draft offered the least liquid sub-sector in fixed income as the answer to "credit spread without taking rate risk", which contradicts this entry's own whenNotTo[3], where spread views go to CDS as cleaner and more liquid. The slot now carries the buy case the candidate is actually graded on and which the entry was missing entirely: the manager expects rate volatility to fall, so buy agency MBS, because holding MBS is being short the prepayment option. Question bank: "Choate expresses his belief that market expectations of interest rate volatility will decrease, so he buys agency MBS" and "an investor buying MBS expects lower, not higher, volatility"; flashcard: "Benefit 2: add exposure to interest rate VOLATILITY through prepayment and extension risk (MBS)" and "higher benchmark yield volatility RAISES the value of the issuer's embedded call, lowering MBS value". The surviving part of the old item, floating-rate CLO collateral, is now stated in the form the flashcard gives it, a CLO tranche beating a CDO tranche when short rates are rising. Lens 1 reached the same gap from cons[4], that negative convexity was filed only as a defect with no mirror recommendation.

Skeptic pass. pros[4]: the taxonomy was garbled and the conclusion inverted. The draft listed "aggregate" as a peer sector of MBS, government, corporate and high yield; the cited reading lists those as index categories ("Bond indexes span many categories, aggregate (broad investment-grade), government, corporate, high-yield, mortgage-backed, and global"), and an aggregate index contains the securitized sector rather than sitting beside it ("a US aggregate spans Treasuries, agencies, corporates, MBS, ABS and CMBS"), so the sentence contradicted itself when it went on to rely on aggregate being the container. "A deliberate sector bet" also inverted the point, since the value of the observation is that the bet is unintended, which cues[4] had right as "not a free decision". Rewritten as an unintended sector bet showing up as tracking error, with the enhanced-indexing matching list the reading supplies. Both skeptics flagged this independently.

Skeptic pass. pros[2]: scoped. The draft asserted the yield pickup as a family-wide property, which contradicts pros[3] two items later and the flashcard "Covered bonds: DUAL recourse ... plus substitution of non-performing assets, lower credit risk and a LOWER yield than ABS/MBS". The notes sentence is hedged ("often a higher yield") and the entry had dropped the hedge. Now hedged, scoped to ABS, CMBS, non-agency RMBS and CLOs, and the covered bond exception stated inline. Both skeptics flagged this claim.

Skeptic pass. pros[0] and cues[0]: the CDO case was missing. The draft caveated only CLOs, naming the weaker case; the question bank keys the stronger one outright, "because the collateral for a CDO consists of its underlying corporate bonds. Accordingly, there is no diversification benefit". Both now say a CDO of corporate bonds adds no collateral diversification at all, that CLOs diversify within corporate credit, and that a covered bond's first recourse is the issuing bank's own credit. The same caveat was added to whenToRecommend[0], which carried the uncaveated claim in a third place. Both skeptics flagged this claim.

Skeptic pass. pros[5]: "little duration" qualified, and the ABS generalisation dropped. Rate duration and spread duration are different exposures and this reading's calculation core is spread duration and DTS, with E(excess return) = (spread x t) minus (spread change x spread duration) minus (t x POD x LGD). A floating-rate tranche resets its coupon, so its rate duration is short, but its spread duration is unchanged and the spread-widening term is untouched. The claim is also now limited to CLOs, since the flashcard attributes floating rates to CLO collateral ("diversified pool of FLOATING-rate leveraged loans") and describes ABS only as consumer receivables, so "many ABS tranches" was an added market-convention generalisation. Both skeptics flagged this claim.

Skeptic pass. pros[3]: the comparator was substituted. The draft said covered bonds "normally price inside the same bank's senior unsecured debt and recover better in default". The candidate is taught the comparison against ABS and MBS, not against another slice of the same bank's debt stack, and the flashcard classifies a covered bond as "bank senior debt backed by a mortgage or public sector pool", so a relative-pricing claim inside one issuer's stack is market convention rather than taught material. Replaced with the taught comparison, lower credit risk and a lower yield than ABS or MBS, and asset substitution added, which the flashcard gives.

Skeptic pass. summary: two overstatements. "The thinnest liquidity in fixed income" generalised past the notes, whose liquidity table has a single bottom row, "Securitized / structured / EM", and whose ranking line is "sovereign > IG > high-yield > securitized/EM", so securitized is bracketed with EM rather than alone at the bottom. This is the same overstatement the repair pass had already corrected in cons[3] and then left standing in the summary. Separately, "can this investor accept cash flow timing the borrower controls" was set up as the single gate for the whole family but is false for covered bonds, which this entry's own whenToRecommend and cues rule in, and it misnames the option holder for CLOs, where the reinvestment and call decisions sit with the manager and equity holders. The timing half is now scoped to the pass-through instruments, with the covered bond exception stated.

Skeptic pass. cues[3]: the implication answered only half its own signal. The signal lists "a Macaulay duration set equal to a horizon", which is single-liability immunization rather than cash-flow matching, and the stated reason, uncertain timing, does not reach it. The immunization reasons are separate and more gradeable, so the implication now gives them: with rate-dependent cash flows you are on effective duration rather than a reliable Macaulay duration, effective duration shortens as rates fall and lengthens as they rise so MacDur(A) equal to the horizon will not hold between rebalances, and negative convexity cannot meet the condition that asset convexity sit just above the liability's.

Skeptic pass. cues[5]: repointed. The signal and implication were a third statement of a point whenToRecommend[2] and pros[1] already carried, the precise risk appetite and the loss ordering, and added nothing. The slot now carries the tranche decision the candidate is actually graded on and which no item in the entry covered: "(a) Recovery / lower-than-expected defaults: move DOWN in tranche, since lower-rated tranches tighten more" and "(b) Housing-led slowdown: move UP within MBS (e.g. BBB tranche to A tranche), this keeps the real-estate cash flow exposure while cutting exposure to the greater spread widening of lower-rated MBS".

Skeptic pass. pitfalls[3]: trimmed. The pitfall's job is to name the marking error, stopping at prepayment, which its first sentence does. The second sentence reprinted the both-directions mechanism from cons[1] six lines earlier, so it is cut.

Skeptic pass. pitfalls[5]: reframed. The draft told the candidate that calling a covered bond a securitization is an error, but the curriculum itself groups covered bonds with ABS, RMBS/CMBS, CLOs and CDOs as structured instruments, and its sentence "Each is TRANCHED so losses hit the equity tranche first and the senior tranche last" sweeps covered bonds into the tranching rule. Nothing in the notes, flashcards or question bank frames the grouping as a marking error, so the pitfall was the entry's own invention and invited the candidate to spend words contradicting the stem. Where the two skeptics differed on the remedy, Lens 1 wanting the "not tranched" claim kept with a note that the candidate's notes line is loose, Lens 2 wanting it reframed or deleted, Lens 2 was followed: the entry no longer takes a side on the label and states the gradeable feature set instead, dual recourse, ring-fenced pool, assets staying with the bank, substitution of non-performing assets, and the lower credit risk and lower yield that follow. The unreconciled conflict in the source material is recorded in residualRisk.

Skeptic pass. cues[4]: added the size of the exposure, roughly a third of a US aggregate index, from the candidate's own flashcard, and the word unintended. The figure sits in the flashcards rather than the notes text, so it is carried in a cue, which has no source field, rather than in the sourced pros[4] sentence.
Skeptic pass. confidence: held at medium, against Lens 2's recommendation to raise it to high. See rejections.

Skeptic pass. residualRisk: replaced. The stated residual risk, that no notes sentence states a yield pickup over corporates, does not exist; the notes state it in those words. See the retraction entry above.
_review.residualRisk: Two items, both about the source material rather than this entry's claims. First, grounding.json's slice for this key is incomplete and should not be trusted for a later pass: it carries 7 note sentences and reports los: [] and counts.los: 0, but it omits the whole dedicated LOS section of fixed_income_active_management_credit_strategies, and los_master.json carries the official LOS fixed_income_active_management_credit_strategies.j, "describe the use of structured financial instruments as an alternative to corporate bonds in credit portfolios", with two graded question-bank items and nine flashcards against it. The repair pass's three false-provenance corrections all trace to that truncated extract. Re-extract before trusting any confidence rating computed from the grounding counts. Second, the candidate's notes and flashcards conflict on one point and the conflict is unresolved in the material: the notes sentence "Each is TRANCHED so losses hit the equity tranche first and the senior tranche last" sweeps covered bonds into the tranching rule, while the flashcard treats a covered bond as single-class bank senior debt with dual recourse. This entry no longer asserts either side, so nothing here is wrong, but a candidate who meets the conflict elsewhere will not be able to tell which line is loose. Also note the LOS verb is "describe", while this entry is written almost entirely as recommend and rule-out, which suits a vignette but is not the verb the essay stem would use.
